title: After the Paper Was Turned Over
teaser: For three afternoons in a row, the tomatoes in the rooftop garden have wilted, and another heat wave is due in four days. Three volunteers must decide whether to water more, water less, or investigate another cause first, while the reliable sources they find are pushing them toward opposite actions.
paragraphs: For the past two weeks, the rooftop garden had run on the same duty sheet: water every morning, then write “watered” in the evening box. On the third afternoon, Kai found more than a dozen tomato plants drooping at once, even though the surface of the potting soil was still wet. The forecast showed another 35°C day in four days. Sumin had already found horticultural guidance saying plants should receive enough water during extreme heat, while an article Xu had saved warned that continuously wet soil could deprive roots of oxygen. Kai carried the worst plant to the tool-room door, wrote “Why are they wilting if we water every day?” on the back of a discarded printout, and pinned the corner down with a pair of scissors.

They first searched separately because it was the fastest approach. Within half an hour they had seven or eight possibilities: shade, potassium deficiency, root rot, drainage, watering time, and more, all from sources that seemed credible. If they followed Sumin’s material alone, adding an afternoon watering made sense. If they followed Xu’s, adding more water could make things worse. More troubling, the duty sheet recorded only “watered.” No one knew how much water each planter had actually received. The pile of information kept growing, but what they should do to the whole garden the next day became no clearer.

Instead of adding more answers to the sheet, they walked the roof again. Most of the tomatoes stood upright in the morning, drooped after two o’clock, and recovered by evening. Two planters against the wall were different: their plants stayed limp into the evening, and the surface soil remained wetter than elsewhere. Kai turned the scrap of paper over. On the back, the three of them wrote only the differences they could confirm together: “most recover by evening,” “two by the wall do not recover,” and “water volume and deeper moisture unknown.” Beneath those notes they added three narrower questions: Which planters dry out deeper down in the afternoon? Which stay wet? Does the difference by location repeat each day? Their earlier sources were not discarded, but from that point on, what they investigated was no longer determined by which explanation each person had believed first.

The next day they still worked separately. Kai searched only for reliable information on temporary heat wilt and evening recovery. Sumin listed field signs of excess moisture, oxygen deprivation, and root problems. Xu measured deeper soil moisture, surface temperature, and drainage speed in different planters. They also called the horticultural adviser who worked with the community, but they did not hand over the problem and ask for a diagnosis. They reported the observations they had agreed on and asked which checks best distinguished short-term water stress from prolonged excess moisture. The adviser told them to focus on deeper moisture, drainage speed, and root condition; the conclusion still had to come from the evidence on site.

By the third afternoon, the three lines on the back of the paper could finally be read against one another. In most planters, the surface was still damp while the deeper soil became noticeably drier in the afternoon, and the plants recovered quickly by evening. The two planters by the wall stayed wet deeper down; one had a drainage hole blocked by leaf fragments, and part of its root system had turned brown. The single symptom of “wilting” had become two treatments that could be tested. The ordinary planters would receive slower, deeper watering early in the morning, with recovery times recorded. The two by the wall would first have their drainage cleared and receive no extra water; one would remain under the adviser’s review. No one lowered the standard of evidence. The difference was that every piece of evidence was now answering the same shared set of questions.

At three o’clock on the hot day, a few plants in the ordinary planters still drooped slightly, but they lifted earlier than on previous days. One planter by the wall had improved; the other remained on its own for observation. Sumin filed the articles they had first found, Xu added that day’s moisture readings, and Kai moved the scissors off the scrap of paper. The question on the front — “Why are they wilting if we water every day?” — was still there. The last line on the back read: “15:00, wall planter No. 2: continue separate observation.”
explanation: The PBL seven-step method begins learning with an open problem. The group first clarifies the situation together, defines the problem, proposes and organizes what it already understands, and then forms learning and verification objectives. Members may then search independently, take measurements, or consult experts before returning to the group to integrate evidence, revise their understanding, and decide on the next action. The key mechanism is not the mechanical completion of seven steps. It is that jointly defining the problem changes the direction of subsequent learning and allows the information members bring back to be compared and integrated around the same question.
mapping: The first round of separate searches produces several reliable but conflicting recommendations → A lack of information is not the only problem; a vague problem definition leads each person to accumulate answers around a different assumption.

“Why are they wilting?” is rewritten in terms of recovery time, deeper soil moisture, and location differences → Joint problem definition creates shared learning objectives and directly changes what evidence the group needs next.

They still divide the work, search independently, measure on site, and consult a horticultural adviser → PBL does not exclude independent learning, expert input, or division of labor; it makes those activities serve a jointly formed problem.

All evidence returns to the same sheet and leads to two different testable treatments → The learning outcome is not a bundle of collected sources, but a revised understanding and course of action produced through joint synthesis.
boundary: PBL is suited to open problems where information is incomplete and members need to learn in order to build a shared understanding. When a task already has a clear standard procedure, time is extremely limited, there is an immediate safety risk, or diagnosis must be performed by a qualified specialist, following the established guidance or escalating directly to an expert is usually more appropriate. Joint inquiry also does not replace standards of evidence. A better-defined problem does not guarantee a correct conclusion.
reflection: If the three volunteers had not turned the paper over and rewritten the problem first, but had simply kept increasing the amount of searching, what would they most likely still be arguing about?
